title: Menopause and weight gain: what happens and what you can do
intro: Many women say, 'I eat the same as before, but my tummy keeps getting bigger.' You are not alone, and this is not because you are lazy. Around menopause, the body goes through many changes. When we understand what is happening, it is easier to take the right steps.

sections.p: Menopause usually happens around age 45 to 55. The hormone oestrogen drops. As a result, fat tends to gather around the tummy. Muscle also decreases as we age, so the body uses slightly less energy than before. Add to that hot flushes at night, disturbed sleep and mood swings. All of these can affect your appetite and your energy to move.

sections.h: Eating: no need for extreme diets
sections.p: Extreme diets can make you lose muscle and feel more tired. Try the quarter-quarter-half plate: half the plate vegetables, a quarter rice, a quarter protein such as fish, chicken, eggs or tofu. Rice is still fine, just control the amount, for example about one medium scoop. You can still enjoy kuih and teh tarik, but maybe not every day, or choose kurang manis (less sweet). Protein at every meal helps you feel full longer and protects your muscle.

sections.h: Move: walk and strengthen your muscles
sections.p: The best combination is walking plus light strength training. Walking helps your heart, blood sugar and mood. Strength exercises like sit-to-stand from a chair, wall push-ups and lifting water bottles help protect muscle and bones. After menopause, bones become more fragile, so weight-bearing exercise like walking helps a lot.

Lack of sleep can make us hungrier and crave sweet food. Try sleeping in a cool room, wear thin sleepwear, and avoid coffee or strong tea after the afternoon. Cut down phone screen time an hour before bed. Stress can also make us eat more without realising. Make time for things that calm you, like an evening walk, gardening or chatting with friends.

sections.h: Measure progress in a fairer way
sections.p: Body weight can go up and down from day to day. Besides the scale, try measuring your waist once a month, and notice how your clothes feel, your energy level and your sleep quality. Progress may be slow, and that is okay. What matters is small habits you can keep up for years.

action: Today, arrange your lunch plate as half vegetables, a quarter rice, a quarter protein.
Walk 15 to 20 minutes, 3 days this week, in the morning or evening.
Do 10 sit-to-stands from a chair and 10 wall push-ups, 2 times a week.
Stop coffee or strong tea after 3pm for one week and notice your sleep.
Measure your waist today and write it down. Measure again after 4 weeks.
doctor: See a doctor if you have vaginal bleeding after your periods have stopped for 12 months or more; if your periods become very heavy, very frequent or badly irregular; if hot flushes and night sweats seriously disturb your sleep and work; if you feel sad or low for a long time; or if your weight rises quickly together with swelling, extreme tiredness or feeling unusually cold. If you want to know about treatment options for menopause symptoms, discuss with your doctor. Do not start, change or stop any medicine on your own.

faq.q: Is weight gain during menopause unavoidable?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Hormone changes do make fat gather more easily around the tummy, but your eating, movement, sleep and stress habits still have a big effect. Small, consistent changes can help, although results differ for each person.

faq.q: Do I need to cut out rice completely?
faq.a: No need. Rice can stay in your diet. Control the portion size, pair it with plenty of vegetables and protein, and try a light walk after eating. This is easier to keep up than stopping rice altogether.

faq.q: I always feel tired. How can I exercise?
faq.a: Start very small, for example 5 to 10 minutes of walking or chair exercises. Many people feel more energetic after a few weeks of moving. But if the tiredness is ongoing and severe, see a doctor to check for other causes like anaemia or thyroid problems.
